claims.text: Nanoscale chemical ordering acts as a structural mediator of strength and deformation in metastable multi-component concentrated alloys.
Nanoscale chemical ordering increases the energy barrier for twin nucleation.
Rapid quenching produces a baseline alloy with minimal chemical ordering.
Thermal treatment promotes nanoscale chemical ordering in the alloy.
Annealed and quenched samples can be compared while holding alloy composition constant.
Room-temperature, moderate-to-high-strain-rate testing promotes metastable twinning in the target alloys.
The degree of nanoscale chemical ordering alters the local energy landscape.
Changes in the local energy landscape caused by chemical ordering can facilitate or impede twin nucleation.
Enhanced chemical ordering locally stabilizes certain atomic configurations.
Local stabilization caused by enhanced ordering raises the twin-nucleation energy barrier.
A higher twin-nucleation barrier delays the onset of deformation twinning.
Delayed deformation twinning modifies work-hardening behavior relative to a disordered structure.
The ordered alloy will have higher yield strength than the disordered baseline.
The ordered alloy will have a higher threshold stress for twin nucleation than the disordered baseline.
The ordered alloy will exhibit reduced twin activity relative to the disordered baseline.
Extreme-temperature or quasi-static deformation may activate mechanisms different from those proposed under room-temperature, moderate-to-high-strain-rate conditions.
Failure to observe both a statistically significant yield-strength increase and delayed or reduced twinning in ordered samples would falsify the hypothesis.
